practice_questions.text: State what is meant by homeostasis.
practice_questions.marks: Homeostasis is the regulation/maintenance of a constant/stable internal environment (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of a synapse in the transmission of a nerve impulse.
practice_questions.marks: When an impulse reaches the end of a neurone, neurotransmitters are released into the synaptic gap (1). These chemicals diffuse across and bind to receptors on the next neurone, triggering a new electrical impulse (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the myelin sheath helps nerve impulses travel efficiently.
practice_questions.marks: The myelin sheath is a fatty/insulating layer around the axon (1). It prevents the electrical impulse from being lost to surrounding tissue (1). This means impulses travel faster along myelinated neurones (1).

practice_questions.text: Compare the roles of sensory neurones and motor neurones in a reflex arc.
practice_questions.marks: Sensory neurones carry impulses from receptors to the CNS (1). Motor neurones carry impulses from the CNS to effectors (1). Both transmit electrical impulses (1). However, they carry signals in opposite directions — sensory towards the CNS, motor away from it (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why reflex actions are important for survival. Use an example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6 marks): Full explanation with a named example, correct reflex arc pathway, and clear link to survival. Secure (3–4 marks): Correct pathway with partial explanation of survival advantage. Developing (1–2 marks): Basic idea that reflexes are fast/automatic. Example points: Reflexes are automatic/involuntary responses (1). They do not involve conscious thought so are very fast (1). Example: touching a hot object — receptor detects heat, impulse travels via sensory neurone to relay neurone in spinal cord, then motor neurone to muscle (effector), hand pulled away (1). The brain is bypassed so response is faster (1). This protects the body from harm/damage (1). Speed of response reduces injury (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the three components of a homeostatic control system.
practice_questions.marks: Receptors detect changes in the environment/stimulus (1). Coordination centres (brain/spinal cord) process the information (1). Effectors (muscles/glands) carry out the response (1).

practice_questions.text: State the energy store associated with a moving object.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark(s) for:
• Kinetic (energy store) (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the energy transfer that occurs when a ball is thrown upwards into the air. Ignore the effects of air resistance.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Energy is transferred from the kinetic store (1)
• to the gravitational potential energy store (1).

practice_questions.text: A catapult is pulled back and used to launch a stone. Explain the energy transfers that take place from the moment the catapult is released.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Energy is transferred from the elastic potential store of the catapult (1)
• to the kinetic store of the stone (1)
• and to the thermal store of the surroundings (due to air resistance/friction) (1).

practice_questions.text: Compare the energy transfers that occur when a car accelerates along a flat road with those when a car drives up a steep hill at constant speed.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Both: energy is transferred from the chemical store of the fuel (1)
• Flat road: energy goes to the kinetic store of the car (1)
• Hill: energy goes to the gravitational potential energy store (as the car gains height) (1)
• Both: some energy is dissipated to the thermal store of the surroundings by heating (friction/air resistance) (1).

practice_questions.text: A student says ‘energy is lost when a light bulb is switched on.’ Explain why this statement is not correct.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Energy cannot be created or destroyed / conservation of energy (1)
• Energy is transferred from the chemical/electrical store to the thermal store of the surroundings (1)
• The energy is dissipated (spread out) rather than lost — it is no longer in a useful form (1).

practice_questions.text: A battery-powered toy car is switched on and travels across a table before falling off the edge. Describe the energy transfers and changes in energy stores from the moment the car is switched on until it hits the ground.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• Chemical store of the battery transfers energy electrically to the kinetic store of the car
• Some energy dissipated to thermal store of surroundings by heating (friction)
• As car leaves the table edge, energy is transferred from the gravitational potential store
• Gravitational potential energy decreases as height decreases
• Kinetic energy increases as the car speeds up while falling
• On impact, kinetic energy is transferred to thermal and elastic potential stores (deformation/sound)

Mastering (5–6 marks): Clear, detailed description of all stages with correct store and pathway names.
Secure (3–4 marks): Most energy stores and transfers correctly identified.
Developing (1–2 marks): Some correct energy stores named but pathways unclear.

practice_questions.text: State the principle of conservation of energy.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark(s) for:
• Energy cannot be created or destroyed (1).

Also accept: the total energy in a closed system remains constant.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways unwanted energy transfers can be reduced in mechanical systems.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Lubrication to reduce friction between moving parts (1)
• Thermal insulation to reduce energy loss by heating (1).

practice_questions.text: A student lifts a 3 kg box to a height of 2 m. Calculate the gravitational potential energy gained. Use \(g = 10\) N/kg.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Writes or identifies \(\Delta GPE = m \times g \times \Delta h\) (1)
• Substitutes correctly: \(3 \times 10 \times 2\) (1)
• Gives correct answer: 60 J (1).

practice_questions.text: A 0.2 kg tennis ball is hit at a speed of 10 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Writes or identifies \(KE = \frac{1}{2} \times m \times v^2\) (1)
• Substitutes correctly: \(\frac{1}{2} \times 0.2 \times 10^2\) (1)
• Gives correct answer: 10 J (1).

practice_questions.text: Compare the use of fossil fuels and wind energy as energy resources.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Fossil fuels are non-renewable / wind is renewable (1)
• Fossil fuels produce CO\(_2\) / greenhouse gases when burned; wind does not (1)
• Fossil fuels provide a reliable / constant supply; wind is intermittent / depends on weather (1)
• Fossil fuels have high energy density per kg; wind turbines require large areas of land (1).

practice_questions.text: A light bulb is supplied with 100 J of energy each second. It transfers 15 J of energy as light and the rest as heat. Calculate the efficiency of the light bulb and explain why no device can ever be 100% efficient.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• Efficiency = useful output ÷ total input = 15 ÷ 100 = 0.15 or 15%
• 85 J is transferred to the thermal store of the surroundings
• This wasted energy is dissipated and cannot easily be recovered
• All devices transfer some energy to thermal stores through friction, air resistance, or electrical resistance
• Conservation of energy means total energy is conserved, but some is always transferred to less useful stores
• Therefore no real device can be 100% efficient

Mastering (5–6 marks): Correct calculation with clear, detailed explanation using correct terminology.
Secure (3–4 marks): Correct calculation with some explanation of wasted energy.
Developing (1–2 marks): Attempts calculation or provides basic explanation.

practice_questions.text: State the name given to the gland that is known as the 'master gland'.
practice_questions.marks: The pituitary gland (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe two effects that adrenaline has on the body during a fight-or-flight response.
practice_questions.marks: Increases heart rate (1). Stimulates the liver to convert glycogen to glucose / raises blood sugar (1). Also accept: increases blood pressure (1) or increases blood flow to muscles (1). Any two for 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Explain the role of negative feedback in the control of thyroxine levels.
practice_questions.marks: When thyroxine levels drop, the hypothalamus releases TRH which stimulates the pituitary to release TSH (1). TSH stimulates the thyroid to produce thyroxine (1). When levels return to normal, thyroxine inhibits TRH and TSH release, preventing overproduction (1).

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Compare the roles of insulin and glucagon in regulating blood glucose concentration.
practice_questions.marks: Insulin is released when blood glucose is too high (1). It causes cells to take up glucose and the liver to convert glucose to glycogen (1). Glucagon is released when blood glucose is too low (1). It stimulates the liver to break down glycogen back into glucose (1).

practice_questions.text: A patient has been diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. Explain the cause of this condition and suggest how it could be managed.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6 marks): Clear explanation of insulin resistance, link to lifestyle factors, and detailed management strategies. Secure (3–4 marks): Correct cause with some management detail. Developing (1–2 marks): Basic understanding that blood glucose is not controlled. Example points: Type 2 diabetes is caused by the body’s cells becoming resistant to insulin (1) or the pancreas not producing enough insulin (1). It is linked to obesity / poor diet / lack of exercise (1). Management includes eating a balanced diet low in sugar (1), taking regular exercise (1) and losing weight (1). Some patients may also need medication (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe how hormones are transported from endocrine glands to target organs.
practice_questions.marks: Hormones are secreted directly into the bloodstream (1). They are carried in the blood to target organs where they have their effect (1).

practice_questions.text: State the name of the hormone that triggers ovulation.
practice_questions.marks: LH / luteinising hormone (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of progesterone in the menstrual cycle.
practice_questions.marks: Progesterone maintains the uterus lining / keeps the uterus lining thick (1). It inhibits the release of FSH and LH / prevents further ovulation (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the combined contraceptive pill prevents pregnancy.
practice_questions.marks: The pill contains oestrogen and progesterone (1). These hormones inhibit FSH, which prevents egg maturation / prevents ovulation (1). They also thicken cervical mucus, making it harder for sperm to reach the egg (1).

practice_questions.text: Compare hormonal and barrier methods of contraception.
practice_questions.marks: Hormonal methods use synthetic hormones to prevent ovulation (1). Barrier methods physically prevent sperm from reaching the egg (1). Hormonal methods are more effective at preventing pregnancy but can have side effects (1). Only barrier methods (condoms) protect against STIs (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain the process of IVF and suggest why it may not be successful on the first attempt.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6 marks): Detailed description of IVF stages with reasoned explanation of why it may fail. Secure (3–4 marks): Correct IVF steps with brief mention of success limitations. Developing (1–2 marks): Basic idea of IVF. Example points: The mother is given FSH and LH to stimulate maturation of multiple eggs (1). Eggs are collected from the ovaries (1). The eggs are fertilised with sperm in a laboratory (1). Fertilised embryos develop for a few days (1). One or two embryos are transferred to the uterus (1). It may fail because the embryo may not implant in the uterus lining (1). Success rate per cycle is relatively low (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the interaction between FSH and oestrogen in the first half of the menstrual cycle.
practice_questions.marks: FSH stimulates the ovary to produce oestrogen (1). Oestrogen causes the uterus lining to thicken / repair (1). Also accept: rising oestrogen stimulates LH release from the pituitary (1). Any two for 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by electric current.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark(s) for:
• The rate of flow of (electric) charge (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe how a voltmeter and an ammeter should be connected in a circuit to measure the potential difference across and current through a resistor.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Ammeter connected in series with the resistor (1)
• Voltmeter connected in parallel across the resistor (1).

practice_questions.text: A 6 V battery pushes a current of 0.3 A through a resistor. Calculate the resistance of the resistor.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Writes or identifies \(R = V \div I\) or \(V = I \times R\) (1)
• Substitutes correctly: \(R = 6 \div 0.3\) (1)
• Gives correct answer: 20 \(\Omega\) (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why the resistance of a filament lamp increases as the current through it increases.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• As current increases, the filament heats up (1)
• The ions in the metal lattice vibrate more (1)
• Electrons collide more frequently with ions, opposing the flow of charge / increasing resistance (1).

practice_questions.text: Compare how the resistance of a thermistor and a light-dependent resistor (LDR) changes with their surroundings.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Thermistor: resistance decreases as temperature increases (1)
• LDR: resistance decreases as light intensity increases (1)
• Both can be used as sensors in control circuits (1)
• Thermistor responds to temperature / LDR responds to light — they measure different physical quantities (1).

practice_questions.text: A student uses a circuit with a battery, ammeter, voltmeter, variable resistor, and a fixed resistor to investigate the I–V characteristics of the fixed resistor. Describe the method the student should use and explain what the results would show.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• Connect ammeter in series with the fixed resistor
• Connect voltmeter in parallel across the fixed resistor
• Use the variable resistor to change the current
• Record pairs of current and potential difference readings
• Plot current on the y-axis against potential difference on the x-axis
• For a fixed resistor (at constant temperature) the graph is a straight line through the origin
• This shows current is directly proportional to potential difference — the resistor obeys Ohm’s law
• The gradient of the line gives 1/R (the reciprocal of resistance)

Mastering (5–6 marks): Clear method and interpretation with correct use of key terms.
Secure (3–4 marks): Method mostly correct with some interpretation of results.
Developing (1–2 marks): Basic method described or some relevant points made.

practice_questions.text: State the complementary base pair for adenine in a DNA molecule.
practice_questions.marks: Thymine (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the structure of a nucleotide.
practice_questions.marks: A nucleotide consists of a sugar (deoxyribose) (1) and a phosphate group (1) with one of four bases (A, T, C, G) attached (1). Any two for 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between genotype and phenotype.
practice_questions.marks: Genotype is the combination of alleles an organism has for a gene (1). Phenotype is the observable physical characteristic (1). The phenotype is determined by the genotype and may also be influenced by environmental factors (1).

practice_questions.text: Two parents are both heterozygous for a trait (Bb). Compare the expected genotypes and phenotypes of their offspring.
practice_questions.marks: The possible genotypes are BB, Bb, Bb and bb (1). The ratio is 1 BB : 2 Bb : 1 bb (1). Three out of four offspring (75%) would be expected to show the dominant phenotype (1). One out of four (25%) would show the recessive phenotype (1).

practice_questions.text: The Human Genome Project mapped the entire human genome. Explain two potential benefits of this project for medicine.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6 marks): Two clear benefits with detailed explanations linked to medicine. Secure (3–4 marks): Two benefits with partial explanation. Developing (1–2 marks): One benefit named. Example points: Scientists can identify genes linked to inherited diseases / genetic disorders (1). This could lead to screening / testing for these conditions before symptoms appear (1). It allows development of personalised medicines based on an individual’s genome (1). It helps understand how genetic variation affects drug responses (1). Understanding the genome helps develop gene therapy to correct faulty genes (1). It can identify people at risk of certain conditions and provide preventive treatment (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between genetic variation and environmental variation.
practice_questions.marks: Genetic variation is caused by differences in DNA / alleles, arising from mutations or sexual reproduction (1). Environmental variation is caused by factors in the organism’s surroundings, such as diet or climate (1).

practice_questions.text: State what happens to the current at a junction in a parallel circuit.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark(s) for:
• The current splits / divides between the branches (1).

Also accept: current is conserved at a junction.

practice_questions.text: Describe the differences between how potential difference behaves in series and parallel circuits.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• In series, the potential difference is shared between components / adds up to the supply voltage (1)
• In parallel, the potential difference is the same across each branch (1).

practice_questions.text: Three resistors of 5 \(\Omega\), 10 \(\Omega\), and 15 \(\Omega\) are connected in series to a 12 V battery. Calculate the total resistance and the current in the circuit.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• \(R_{\text{total}} = 5 + 10 + 15 = 30 \; \Omega\) (1)
• Uses \(I = V \div R\) (1)
• \(I = 12 \div 30 = 0.4\) A (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why adding more resistors in parallel to a circuit decreases the total resistance.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Adding more branches provides more/additional paths for the current to flow through (1)
• More current can flow from the supply (1)
• Since \(R = V \div I\), if current increases and voltage stays the same, total resistance decreases (1).

practice_questions.text: A 2 A current flows through a 10 \(\Omega\) heater for 60 seconds. Calculate the power of the heater and the total energy transferred.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Uses \(P = I^2 \times R\) (1)
• \(P = 2^2 \times 10 = 40\) W (1)
• Uses \(E = P \times t\) (1)
• \(E = 40 \times 60 = 2400\) J (1).

practice_questions.text: Two identical lamps are first connected in series and then in parallel to the same 12 V battery. Compare the brightness of the lamps and the total current from the battery in each arrangement. Explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• In series, the 12 V is shared equally between the two lamps (6 V each)
• Total resistance in series is higher (R + R = 2R), so less current flows
• Less current and less voltage per lamp means less power per lamp, so they are dimmer
• In parallel, each lamp has the full 12 V across it
• Total resistance is lower (R/2), so more current flows from the battery
• Each lamp has full voltage and more current, so greater power and brighter
• Lamps in parallel are brighter and the total current from the battery is higher

Mastering (5–6 marks): Clear comparison with correct use of series/parallel rules, power reasoning, and relevant equations.
Secure (3–4 marks): Most rules applied correctly with some comparison of brightness.
Developing (1–2 marks): Basic understanding of one arrangement or some correct points.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'variation'.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark:
• The differences in characteristics between individuals of the same species (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe two sources of genetic variation in a population.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks (any two from):
• Mutations cause random changes in DNA / can produce new alleles (1)
• Sexual reproduction mixes alleles from two parents (1)
• Meiosis produces gametes with different combinations of alleles (1)
• Random fertilisation creates unique offspring (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain how natural selection leads to evolution in a population.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Individuals show variation in characteristics (1)
• Those best suited to the environment are more likely to survive and reproduce (1)
• They pass on the alleles for advantageous characteristics to offspring, so over generations the allele becomes more common / the population evolves (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain how the development of antibiotic-resistant bacteria provides evidence for Darwin's theory of natural selection.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Random mutation in a bacterium gives resistance to an antibiotic (1)
• When the antibiotic is used, non-resistant bacteria are killed but the resistant one survives and reproduces (1)
• The resistance allele is passed to offspring, so the resistant strain becomes more common / this shows natural selection in action (1)

practice_questions.text: Compare natural selection and selective breeding.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Natural selection is driven by the environment / selective breeding is driven by humans (1)
• Both involve organisms with certain characteristics being more likely to reproduce (1)
• Natural selection takes many generations / selective breeding can produce rapid changes (1)
• Selective breeding reduces genetic variation because only the chosen parents breed (1)

practice_questions.text: A species of beetle lives on an island. A volcanic eruption splits the island in two, separating the beetle population. Explain how this could eventually lead to two new species of beetle.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Clear explanation covering geographic isolation, different environmental conditions on each island, different selection pressures favouring different characteristics, allele frequencies changing over generations, and eventually the two populations becoming so different they can no longer interbreed — speciation.

Secure (3–4 marks): Explains that the populations are separated and experience different conditions leading to different characteristics, with some reference to natural selection and becoming different species.

Developing (1–2 marks): Identifies that the populations are separated and may become different, but lacks detail about the mechanism of natural selection or speciation.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a polymer.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark(s) for:
• A large molecule made from many small repeating units / monomers joined together (1)

Accept: A long-chain molecule formed by joining many monomers.

practice_questions.text: Describe how addition polymerisation occurs using ethene as an example.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Many ethene molecules / monomers join together (1)
• The carbon–carbon double bond in each ethene opens / breaks and a new single bond forms with the next monomer (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain why alkenes can undergo addition polymerisation but alkanes cannot.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Alkenes contain a carbon–carbon double bond / are unsaturated (1)
• The double bond can open / break to allow bonding with other monomers (1)
• Alkanes only have single bonds / are saturated, so they cannot open a bond for addition (1)

practice_questions.text: Compare the properties of poly(ethene) and PVC and explain why they are used for different purposes.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Poly(ethene) is flexible and waterproof (1)
• So it is used for plastic bags / bottles / packaging (1)
• PVC is rigid and durable (1)
• So it is used for window frames / pipes / guttering (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain why the disposal of synthetic polymers is a problem for the environment.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Most synthetic polymers are not biodegradable (1)
• They persist in landfill / the environment for hundreds of years (1)
• Burning / incinerating polymers can release toxic gases such as carbon monoxide or hydrogen chloride (1)

practice_questions.text: Ethene is produced by cracking larger hydrocarbons. Explain why cracking is necessary and how the ethene produced can be used to make polymers.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• Cracking breaks down larger, less useful hydrocarbons into smaller, more useful molecules
• There is greater demand for shorter-chain hydrocarbons / fuels than for long-chain fractions
• Cracking produces alkenes (such as ethene) as well as shorter alkanes
• Ethene is an unsaturated monomer with a C=C double bond
• Many ethene monomers undergo addition polymerisation
• The double bonds open and monomers join to form poly(ethene)

Mastering (5–6): Clear, logical explanation linking cracking to monomer production and polymerisation, with correct terminology.
Secure (3–4): Describes cracking producing alkenes and that these can polymerise, but may lack detail on mechanism.
Developing (1–2): Identifies that cracking produces useful molecules or that polymers are made from monomers, but limited detail.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by an induced magnet.
practice_questions.marks: • A material that becomes magnetic only when placed in a magnetic field (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the shape and direction of the magnetic field around a bar magnet.
practice_questions.marks:
• Field lines curve from the north pole to the south pole outside the magnet (1).
• Lines are closest together at the poles where the field is strongest (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why a compass needle always points towards geographic north.
practice_questions.marks:
• The Earth’s core is magnetic / the Earth has a magnetic field (1).
• The geographic North Pole is near a magnetic south pole (1).
• The north-seeking pole of the compass needle is attracted towards the magnetic south pole near geographic north (1).

practice_questions.text: Compare permanent magnets and electromagnets. In your answer, explain one advantage of each.
practice_questions.marks:
• A permanent magnet produces its own field continuously without a power supply (1).
• An electromagnet only produces a field when current flows through it (1).
• Advantage of permanent magnet: always on, no electricity needed, e.g. compass (1).
• Advantage of electromagnet: can be switched on and off, e.g. scrapyard crane (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how the magnetic field inside a solenoid is produced when a current flows through it.
practice_questions.marks:
• Each turn/loop of the coil produces its own circular magnetic field (1).
• Inside the solenoid, these fields from individual coils add together (1).
• This creates a strong, almost uniform field along the centre of the solenoid (1).

practice_questions.text: A student wants to design a strong electromagnet for a science project. Explain the factors that affect the strength of an electromagnet, and describe how the student could test whether changes to the design increase its strength.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Clearly explains all three factors (current, turns, iron core) with correct physics. Describes a valid method to test strength, e.g. counting paper clips picked up. Logically structured.

Secure (3–4 marks): Explains at least two factors correctly. Describes a basic method for testing.

Developing (1–2 marks): Identifies one factor. May attempt a test but description is vague or incomplete.

practice_questions.text: State how you can use melting point data to determine whether a substance is pure.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark(s) for:
• A pure substance has a sharp / fixed / exact melting point (1)

Accept: A mixture melts over a range of temperatures.

practice_questions.text: Describe how paper chromatography is used to separate the dyes in an ink.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• A spot of ink is placed on a pencil baseline on chromatography paper, which is placed in a solvent (1)
• The solvent rises up the paper and carries the dyes to different heights / different dyes move at different rates (1)

practice_questions.text: A substance in a chromatogram moved 4.2 cm. The solvent front moved 6.0 cm. Calculate the Rf value and explain what it tells you about the substance.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Rf = 4.2 / 6.0 (1)
• Rf = 0.7 (1)
• This value can be compared with known Rf values to identify the substance / it shows the substance is fairly soluble in the mobile phase (1)

practice_questions.text: Compare filtration and crystallisation as methods for separating mixtures.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Filtration separates an insoluble solid from a liquid (1)
• The solid is trapped on the filter paper and the liquid passes through (1)
• Crystallisation obtains a dissolved / soluble solid from a solution (1)
• The solution is heated to evaporate solvent, then cooled to form crystals (1)

practice_questions.text: Describe the chemical tests and expected results for oxygen and carbon dioxide.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Oxygen relights a glowing splint (1)
• Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky / cloudy white (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain how potable water is produced from fresh water sources in the UK. Include why each stage is necessary.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• Sedimentation: large solid particles settle out of the water
• Filtration: removes fine / smaller particles from the water
• Chlorination: kills harmful bacteria / microorganisms to make the water safe to drink
• Potable water is not chemically pure but has sufficiently low levels of dissolved salts and microbes
• In areas without fresh water, distillation or reverse osmosis can be used but these require large amounts of energy
• Water for chemical analysis must be free of dissolved salts to avoid interference with results

Mastering (5–6): Describes all three stages with reasons, distinguishes potable from pure, and may reference alternative methods.
Secure (3–4): Describes at least two stages with reasons for their use.
Developing (1–2): Identifies one or two stages but limited explanation of why they are necessary.

practice_questions.text: State one reason why the five-kingdom classification system was replaced by the three-domain system.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark:
• Genetic analysis / DNA sequencing showed that Archaea are fundamentally different from Bacteria (1).

Accept: chemical/genetic differences between Archaea and Bacteria were discovered.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Describe the role of restriction enzymes and ligase in genetic engineering.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Restriction enzymes cut DNA at specific sequences / cut out the desired gene, leaving sticky ends (1)
• Ligase joins / seals the gene into the vector by bonding the DNA backbones together (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain how genetic analysis provides more accurate classification of organisms than using physical features alone.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Physical features can be misleading due to convergent evolution / unrelated organisms may look similar (1)
• DNA/genetic analysis compares base sequences directly (1)
• The more similar the DNA, the more closely related the organisms are / gives a more accurate picture of evolutionary relationships (1)

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Explain why sticky ends are important in genetic engineering.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Sticky ends are short, unpaired sections of DNA bases (1)
• They allow the gene and vector to join because their bases are complementary / they pair up (1)
• Ligase can then seal the backbone, permanently inserting the gene into the vector (1)

practice_questions.text: Compare the five-kingdom classification system with the three-domain system.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Five kingdoms based on physical features / three domains based on genetic analysis (1)
• Five kingdoms grouped all prokaryotes together / three domains separate Archaea from Bacteria (1)
• Both systems group organisms based on shared characteristics (1)
• Three-domain system better reflects evolutionary relationships / is more scientifically accurate (1)

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the use of genetic engineering in modern agriculture and medicine. Include both benefits and risks in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Balanced evaluation covering specific benefits (e.g. insulin production in bacteria, pest-resistant crops, improved yields) and risks (e.g. gene flow to wild populations, ethical concerns, unknown long-term effects). Reaches a supported conclusion.

Secure (3–4 marks): Identifies several benefits and risks with some specific examples. May lack balance or a clear conclusion.

Developing (1–2 marks): Lists some benefits or risks but lacks detail, specific examples, or evaluation.

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) State what is meant by the motor effect.
practice_questions.marks: • The force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field (1).

practice_questions.text: (Separate Physics only) Describe the role of the split-ring commutator in an electric motor.
practice_questions.marks:
• It reverses the direction of the current every half turn (1).
• This keeps the coil spinning in the same direction continuously (1).

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) A wire of length 0.20 m carries a current of 5 A in a magnetic field of flux density 0.4 T. Calculate the force on the wire. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
• Recall or state F = B × I × l (1).
• Substitution: F = 0.4 × 5 × 0.20 (1).
• Answer: F = 0.4 N (1).

practice_questions.text: Compare a step-up transformer and a step-down transformer. In your answer, refer to the number of turns, the voltage, and the current.
practice_questions.marks:
• Step-up has more turns on secondary than primary / step-down has fewer turns on secondary (1).
• Step-up increases voltage / step-down decreases voltage (1).
• Step-up decreases current / step-down increases current (1).
• In both, power in = power out (for 100% efficiency) / Vₚ × Iₚ = Vₛ × Iₛ (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why electricity is transmitted at high voltage in the national grid.
practice_questions.marks:
• High voltage means a lower current for the same power (1).
• Lower current means less energy lost / wasted as heat in the cables (1).
• This makes transmission more efficient / reduces energy waste (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe how electromagnetic induction works and explain how this principle is used in a transformer to change the voltage of an alternating supply.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Clearly explains electromagnetic induction (changing magnetic field induces a p.d. in a conductor). Describes transformer structure (primary/secondary coils, iron core). Explains how alternating current in the primary creates a changing magnetic field that induces a voltage in the secondary. Links number of turns to voltage change. Well-structured.

Secure (3–4 marks): Describes electromagnetic induction and transformer structure. May miss the role of the changing magnetic field or the link between turns and voltage.

Developing (1–2 marks): Identifies that transformers change voltage or that induction involves magnets and wires, but explanation is incomplete.

practice_questions.text: State the equation linking density, mass, and volume.
practice_questions.marks: • Density = mass ÷ volume / ρ = m/V (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the arrangement and movement of particles in a gas.
practice_questions.marks:
• Particles are far apart / randomly arranged (1).
• They move rapidly in random directions / with high kinetic energy (1).

practice_questions.text: A block of metal has a mass of 540 g and a volume of 200 cm³. Calculate the density of the metal in g/cm³. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
• Recall or write ρ = m/V (1).
• Substitution: ρ = 540/200 (1).
• Answer: ρ = 2.7 g/cm³ (1).

practice_questions.text: Compare specific heat capacity and specific latent heat. In your answer, explain what each measures and give the equation for each.
practice_questions.marks:
• Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg by 1 °C (1).
• Equation: ΔQ = m × c × Δθ (1).
• Specific latent heat is the energy needed to change the state of 1 kg without changing temperature (1).
• Equation: Q = m × L (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why the pressure of a gas in a sealed container increases when the gas is heated.
practice_questions.marks:
• Heating gives particles more kinetic energy / they move faster (1).
• Particles collide with the container walls more frequently and with greater force (1).
• The volume is constant, so the increased rate and force of collisions increases the pressure (1).

practice_questions.text: A student heats 2 kg of water from 20 °C to 100 °C using an immersion heater. The specific heat capacity of water is 4200 J/kg °C and the specific latent heat of vaporisation is 2,260,000 J/kg. Calculate the total energy needed to heat the water to 100 °C and then boil all of it. Show all your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Correctly calculates heating energy (ΔQ = 2 × 4200 × 80 = 672,000 J) and boiling energy (Q = 2 × 2,260,000 = 4,520,000 J). Adds both: total = 5,192,000 J. Clear working shown.

Secure (3–4 marks): Correctly calculates one part (either heating or boiling). May make an error in the other or fail to add them.

Developing (1–2 marks): Selects the correct equations but substitution or arithmetic contains errors.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'community'.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark:
• All the populations of different species living and interacting in the same area (1).

Accept: all the organisms of different species in an ecosystem/habitat.

practice_questions.text: Describe one example of mutualism.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Named example, e.g. mycorrhizal fungi and plant roots (1)
• Both organisms benefit: fungi help plant absorb minerals / plant gives fungi sugars (1)

Accept other valid examples with both organisms and both benefits named.

practice_questions.text: Explain how eutrophication leads to the death of fish in a river.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Excess nutrients (e.g. from fertilisers) cause rapid growth of algae / algal bloom (1)
• Algae block light to aquatic plants, which die / bacteria decompose dead organisms (1)
• Decomposing bacteria use up dissolved oxygen, so fish suffocate (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain how you would use quadrats to estimate the population of dandelions in a school field.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Place quadrats randomly across the field / use random number coordinates (1)
• Count the dandelions in each quadrat and calculate the mean per quadrat (1)
• Multiply the mean by the total area of the field divided by the quadrat area to estimate total population (1)

practice_questions.text: Compare the effects of abiotic and biotic factors on a community.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Abiotic factors are non-living (e.g. temperature, light, water) / biotic factors are living (e.g. competition, predation) (1)
• Both types of factor affect the distribution and abundance of organisms (1)
• Abiotic factors affect physical conditions / biotic factors involve interactions between organisms (1)
• Example of each: temperature limits enzyme activity / predators reduce prey populations (1)

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the importance of maintaining biodiversity. Refer to both local and global examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Detailed evaluation explaining why biodiversity matters (ecosystem stability, food webs, medicines, resources), with specific examples of local conservation (nature reserves, breeding programmes) and global efforts (reforestation, international agreements). Discusses consequences of biodiversity loss.

Secure (3–4 marks): Explains some benefits of maintaining biodiversity with examples at local or global level. May lack balance between local and global or be less detailed.

Developing (1–2 marks): States that biodiversity is important with limited explanation or examples.

practice_questions.text: State one gas that was present in large amounts in the Earth’s early atmosphere.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark(s) for:
• Carbon dioxide (1)

Also accept: water vapour.

practice_questions.text: Describe how the level of oxygen in the Earth’s atmosphere increased over time.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Primitive plants / algae evolved and carried out photosynthesis (1)
• Photosynthesis absorbed carbon dioxide and released oxygen into the atmosphere (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain how the greenhouse effect keeps the Earth warm.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Short-wavelength radiation from the Sun passes through the atmosphere and warms the Earth’s surface (1)
• The Earth re-radiates longer-wavelength infrared radiation (1)
• Greenhouse gases (e.g. CO₂, methane, water vapour) absorb and re-emit this infrared radiation, warming the atmosphere (1)

practice_questions.text: Compare the composition of the Earth’s early atmosphere with today’s atmosphere.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Early atmosphere had high levels of carbon dioxide / today has only about 0.04% CO₂ (1)
• Early atmosphere had little or no oxygen / today has about 21% oxygen (1)
• Early atmosphere contained water vapour which condensed to form oceans (1)
• Today’s atmosphere is mainly nitrogen (~78%) and oxygen (~21%) (1)

practice_questions.text: Describe the chemical test for oxygen and state the expected result.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Place a glowing splint into the gas (1)
• If oxygen is present, the splint relights (1)

practice_questions.text: Evaluate the evidence that human activity is the main cause of climate change.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• Burning fossil fuels releases CO₂, increasing its concentration in the atmosphere
• Livestock farming increases methane levels
• There is a strong correlation between increased fossil fuel use, rising CO₂ concentration and rising global temperatures
• Temperature data over the past 150 years shows a clear warming trend that matches the increase in CO₂
• However, there are uncertainties: measurements vary by location, and historical records are less accurate
• Some natural factors (volcanic activity, solar output) also affect climate, so the correlation does not prove causation on its own
• The overwhelming scientific consensus is that human activity is the dominant cause

Mastering (5–6): Evaluates both sides using specific evidence, discusses correlations and uncertainties, and reaches a supported conclusion.
Secure (3–4): Identifies human causes and some evidence, with limited discussion of uncertainties.
Developing (1–2): States that burning fossil fuels causes climate change but provides little supporting evidence or evaluation.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the elastic limit of a spring.
practice_questions.marks: • The maximum force or extension beyond which the spring no longer returns to its original length / no longer obeys Hooke’s law (1).

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between elastic distortion and inelastic distortion.
practice_questions.marks:
• In elastic distortion, the object returns to its original shape when the force is removed (1).
• In inelastic distortion, the object is permanently deformed / does not return to its original shape (1).

practice_questions.text: A spring has a spring constant of 50 N/m. A force of 8 N is applied to the spring. Calculate the extension of the spring. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
• Recall F = k × x, rearrange to x = F/k (1).
• Substitution: x = 8/50 (1).
• Answer: x = 0.16 m (1).

practice_questions.text: Compare the force-extension graphs of a spring obeying Hooke’s law and a rubber band. Explain the key differences.
practice_questions.marks:
• Spring: straight line through the origin (up to elastic limit) / linear relationship (1).
• Rubber band: curved graph / non-linear relationship from the start (1).
• Spring: gradient = spring constant / constant gradient in the linear region (1).
• Rubber band: does not obey Hooke’s law but still returns to original shape / elastic but non-linear (1).

practice_questions.text: A spring with a spring constant of 60 N/m is extended by 0.20 m. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored in the spring.
practice_questions.marks:
• Recall E = ½ × k × x² (1).
• Substitution: E = 0.5 × 60 × 0.20² = 0.5 × 60 × 0.04 (1).
• Answer: E = 1.2 J (1).

practice_questions.text: A student carries out an experiment to investigate how the extension of a spring changes with the applied force. Describe the method the student should use, explain how they would identify the elastic limit from their results, and suggest how they could improve the accuracy of their measurements.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Clearly describes the method (hang spring, add masses, measure extension, calculate from original length). Explains that the elastic limit is where the graph curves / the spring no longer returns to its original length. Suggests improvements (e.g. eye-level reading, repeat and mean, wait for oscillation to stop). Logically structured.

Secure (3–4 marks): Describes the basic method and identifies the elastic limit from the graph. May suggest one improvement.

Developing (1–2 marks): Describes a basic method but omits key details. Does not clearly identify the elastic limit or suggest improvements.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a finite resource.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark(s) for:
• A resource that is being used up faster than it can be replaced / a non-renewable resource (1)

Accept: A resource that will eventually run out.

practice_questions.text: Describe what a life cycle assessment involves.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• It assesses the environmental impact of a product at every stage of its life (1)
• From extracting raw materials, through manufacturing and use, to disposal (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain two advantages of recycling metals compared to extracting them from their ores.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Recycling uses less energy than extraction from ore (1)
• This reduces CO₂ emissions / costs less (1)
• It conserves finite resources / reduces the amount of ore that needs to be mined / reduces landfill waste (1)

practice_questions.text: (Higher tier) Compare phytoextraction and bioleaching as methods of metal extraction.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Phytoextraction uses plants to absorb metal compounds from the soil (1)
• Bioleaching uses bacteria to produce acidic solutions that dissolve metal compounds (1)
• Both are slower than traditional mining methods (1)
• Both have lower environmental impact / can extract metals from low-grade ores (1)

practice_questions.text: Describe the ‘three Rs’ strategy for reducing the use of finite resources.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks (any two of three):
• Reduce — use fewer resources / less packaging (1)
• Reuse — use items again rather than disposing of them (1)
• Recycle — collect and reprocess materials to make new products (1)

practice_questions.text: A company claims their new product is ‘environmentally friendly’ based on a life cycle assessment. Evaluate the reliability of this claim.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• A life cycle assessment considers all stages: raw materials, manufacturing, use and disposal
• The company should have assessed environmental impact at each stage, including energy use, emissions, waste and resource depletion
• Some impacts are difficult to quantify (e.g. biodiversity loss, visual pollution), making the assessment less objective
• Different assessors may give different weightings to different impacts, introducing subjectivity / bias
• The company may have selectively presented data (greenwashing) to make the product look better
• To evaluate the claim, we would need to see the full LCA data, including what was measured and how

Mastering (5–6): Discusses the strengths of LCA methodology alongside its limitations (subjectivity, selective data), and considers what additional information would be needed.
Secure (3–4): Identifies that LCAs have limitations and that some data may be biased, but may not explain in detail.
Developing (1–2): States that a life cycle assessment looks at environmental impacts but provides limited evaluation.

practice_questions.text: Give the name of trophic level 1 in a food chain.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark:
• Producer(s) (1).

Accept: plants / algae.

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of decomposers in the carbon cycle.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks:
• Decomposers (bacteria and fungi) break down dead organic matter (1)
• They respire, releasing carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain why food chains rarely have more than four or five trophic levels.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Energy is lost at each trophic level (1)
• Energy is lost through respiration / heat / movement / not all parts eaten (1)
• By the fourth or fifth level, there is not enough energy to support a viable population (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain how nitrates are made available for plant uptake in the soil.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 3 marks:
• Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert atmospheric nitrogen into ammonia / nitrates (1)
• Decomposers break down dead organisms; nitrifying bacteria convert ammonia to nitrates (1)
• Farmers add fertilisers containing nitrates / use crop rotation with leguminous plants (1)

practice_questions.text: Compare the roles of photosynthesis and respiration in the carbon cycle.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Photosynthesis removes CO₂ from the atmosphere / respiration releases CO₂ into the atmosphere (1)
• Photosynthesis converts CO₂ into glucose (organic compounds) / respiration breaks down glucose to release energy (1)
• Only producers carry out photosynthesis / all living organisms carry out respiration (1)
• Both are essential for carbon cycling between living and non-living parts of the ecosystem (1)

practice_questions.text: Explain how human activities have affected the carbon cycle and suggest how the impact could be reduced.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Clear explanation that burning fossil fuels releases carbon that was locked away for millions of years, increasing atmospheric CO₂, which enhances the greenhouse effect. Deforestation reduces photosynthesis, removing fewer CO₂. Suggests specific solutions: reforestation to absorb CO₂, renewable energy to reduce fossil fuel burning, carbon capture. Links causes to consequences clearly.

Secure (3–4 marks): Identifies that burning fossil fuels increases CO₂ and deforestation reduces CO₂ absorption. Suggests at least one solution with some explanation.

Developing (1–2 marks): States that humans produce more CO₂ or that pollution is a problem, with limited detail or solutions.
